title: NP certificates for homeomorphism of three-manifolds
formal: Does homeomorphism of connected compact triangulated 3-manifolds, allowing boundary and nonorientable manifolds, have polynomially bounded certificates verifiable in polynomial time? Precisely, do there exist a polynomial \(p\) and a uniform deterministic polynomial-time verifier \(V\) such that for every promised pair \((T,U)\in\mathcal D\) of total encoded length \(N\), \[H(T,U)\iff\exists w\in\{0,1\}^{\leq p(N)}\;V(T,U,w)=1?\] This is the NP-certificate question for the promised homeomorphism problem below.
why: Short certificates would separate the cost of discovering topological equivalence from the cost of checking it. An NP upper bound would place a fundamental classification problem within the standard theory of efficient verification.
status_note: The NP question is explicit in the 2024 report and Jackson’s 2024/2025 article. The bounded later-work review through 14 September 2026 found no general certificate theorem. The stated target retains the source’s broad compact connected domain; closed-oriented and Seifert results are limited to their published hypotheses.

progress.text: Kuperberg establishes elementary-recursive decidability for the closed oriented setting.

importance.reason: A major unresolved verification bound for topological classification in dimension three, beyond decidability and the recognition of specific manifold classes.

sentences: Two triangulations can describe the same three-dimensional manifold while looking combinatorially unrelated.
This question asks whether every homeomorphic pair has a certificate whose size and verification time are polynomial in the input.
Such a certificate need not be found efficiently by the verifier itself.
The challenge is to encode the necessary topological equivalence without an excessively long sequence of transformations.
An NP upper bound would distinguish the difficulty of discovering a homeomorphism from the difficulty of checking convincing evidence that one exists.

definitions: A triangulation consists of \(t\geq1\) labelled copies of \(\Delta^3=\{x\in\mathbb R^4:x_i\geq0,\ \sum_{i=0}^3x_i=1\}\), with some triangular faces paired by affine bijections specified by permutations of their three vertices. Each face is unpaired or paired with one other face; a pairing to the identical face slot is forbidden, pairings are reciprocal, and different faces of the same tetrahedron may be paired. The realization \(|T|\) is the disjoint union of the tetrahedra modulo the stated identifications, with the quotient topology. The input promise is that each realization is a nonempty connected compact 3-manifold, possibly with boundary: every point has a neighborhood homeomorphic to an open subset of \(\mathbb R^3\) or of \(\mathbb R^2\times[0,\infty)\). Orientability is not promised and no orientation, boundary marking or distinguished submanifold is supplied. Homeomorphism means a continuous bijection with continuous inverse, with no orientation-preserving or boundary-label requirement. In dimension three this agrees with equivalence of PL triangulations; combinatorial isomorphism of the supplied tetrahedron lists is not required. For a concrete binary encoding, write \(t\) in unary followed by the \(4t\) face slots in label order, each recording an unpaired flag or a partner tetrahedron index, a two-bit face index and one of the six vertex permutations; tetrahedron indices use \(\lceil\log_2(t+1)\rceil\) bits. The two encodings are concatenated and their total bit length is \(N\). Let \(\mathcal D\) be the promised domain of such pairs and \(H(T,U)\) the assertion \(|T|\cong|U|\). Algorithms and verifiers are uniform deterministic multitape Turing machines with bit-operation cost, no advice, oracles or randomness. The certificate statements concern this promised domain: verifiers must halt in their polynomial time bound on all bit strings, but acceptance outside \(\mathcal D\) has no specified topological meaning.
answer_criterion: Prove or refute the displayed existence of \(p,V\) with a complete Lean-checked proof. A positive answer needs completeness for every homeomorphic promised pair and soundness against every candidate witness for every nonhomeomorphic promised pair, with polynomial worst-case verification time in \(N+|w|\). The verifier need not find the witness. A negative answer must exclude all polynomially bounded certificate systems in this model, not merely certificates made from a particular type of topological transformation. A result restricted to a fixed manifold, orientable closed manifolds, or one geometric class does not settle the full domain.

context_blocks.text: Schleimer’s Question 3 asks whether Homeo(3) lies in NP. His standing domain is compact connected manifolds supplied by triangulations. The boundary, orientation and binary-verifier conventions above make that domain explicit.

Two very different tetrahedron lists can describe the same space. A positive certificate must establish equality of the represented topological types, rather than just exhibit a relabelling of the supplied pieces. Its form is unrestricted; the polynomial bound concerns the entire witness and its verification.

Kuperberg proves an elementary-recursive decision algorithm for closed oriented 3-manifolds: the running time has a fixed-height exponential-tower bound. This establishes a quantitative decidability result in that setting, not polynomial certificates for the broader domain.

Jackson proves NP recognition for compact orientable Seifert fibered spaces with nonempty boundary, together with NP and coNP certification for their naming problem. The paper explicitly asks about general homeomorphism, which its special-class results do not decide.

NP verification concerns yes instances. It does not imply a polynomial-time method for constructing a homeomorphism, nor provide short certificates when the manifolds differ. The latter is the separate coNP question.

The 2025 seminar report asks a related fixed-parameter tractability question measured by the treewidth of the input triangulations. A parameter-dependent algorithm with no global polynomial bound would not by itself resolve this certificate question.
